INTERNATIONAL POLICY.

IT is time that English workmen should
form opinions and make their voices heard
upon some of the simpler questions of Infer-
national Policy. Some of these, like that of
Gibraltar, which 1 shall write about next week,
are very simple, while others involve a long
history of rapacity and crime. But it is to
the East rather than to the West that we
hhouhl direct our attention and efforts. The
peoples of the East are weak and we are strong.
Where they are not directly dependent

upon us and part of our Empire, they are at
the mercy of our soldiers and sailors, and of our
mercantile and political rulers. If English
working men are too much engrossed in the
industrial movement here, too much ooeupied
with their own concerns, with their work and
own internal affairs, to take the trouble to in-
quire about and :denounce the misuse of our
power in the East, they neglect that which is
in my eyes one Of their most sacred duties. It

is their function and their duty to insist, by
all the means at their command, that right
shall be done, and that our political action shall
always be subordinated to moral considera-
tions. Now Ido not mean merely that the

grosser forms of cruelty committed by Eng-
lishmen should be denounced and put a atop
to; such as the horrible murders committed in
Jamaica ; the blowing living men from the
mouths of cannon, or the flogging men before
:hanging them, as was done by order of
Our commanding officers in India. Of course,
'these crimes should be punishod. I read this
'very morning in the Times telegram, that a
Mr. COWAN has blown something like fifty
living men from cannon. At present, let
working men remember that these kind of
atrocities go unpunished, and they go
unpunished because our tiuthorities, our
Political rulers, do not regard these things
in their true light; because political conduct
hal,i never been regulated by a pure and high
morality. The persons who commit such
horrible atrocities should be severely punished.
But what I am saying noVr is something far
wider and more general; it is that our whole
national conduct and life towards other-nations,
both in the West and in the East, should be
morally revolutionised, should be replaeedby a
policy consistent with justice, noble and
generous, worthy of our great power, of our
advanced civilisation, worthy of the great
En gl ish people.

It is, however, still the popular creed that
England is right to gratify her propensities at
the expense of other peoples; that anything
she may do to make herself greater or stronger
must be right. Englishmen have not yet
abandoned the belief that England's mission is
°011(1110st and empire, her glory that of military

renown and being mistress of the Seas. They
still look back with pride upon such things as
the battles of Crecy and Poictiers, upon inva-
sions and occupations of foreign countries, for
which there never was a shadow of a justifi-
cation, and for some of which we have still to
atone. Some people call the wretched pride
we take in trampling upon weak nations like
the Chinese, Patriotism. It was the English
Government, which, by wresting an indem-
nity from the C4neso for a war in which we,
wore entirely in the wrong, established as a
precedent that a conquering nation may compel
a conquered nation to pay the costs of the.war ;
an example which Prussia has followed by the
exaction of the most iniquitous and crushing
indemnity from France. And against this
we could not even utter a protest because we had
been guilty of the same crime, because we had
set the example.

England's reputation does. not depend on
brute :force, or iron-clads; or. Armstrong
guns;
.her title to greatness is not war or
buccaneering. Her glory in the past, and I
trust in the future, is that of . leading, with
other nations of the West, the civilisation of the
world; of having created a great industrial
activity; of having produced a noble litera-
ture, and splendid contributions to science,
philosophy, and att. The future task which
England has to perform, is that of carrying to
the less civilised races the results of industry and
knowledge, discovered and wrought out with
so much cost and labour. And this:she has to
accomplish not by arms or force, but by means
• suited to an era of peace and industry. The
time has not yet arrived at which this can be
adequately done. We,, ourselves, are . torn to
pieces by our political and religious differ'ences. The social difficulties which surround
and threaten us at the present moment, are,
such as to demand all the energy of which 'We

are capable. As yet England has brought
little but war and misery to Eastern nations;

in many oases it has been evil unmitigated by

any corresponding good. Terrible effects have
followed upon our mercantile undertakings,

and upon almost all the contact of ,Eastern

nations with Western civilisation. We have
no recognised standard of conduct, no true
poliey to direct and control our actions towards
other nations. I put aside the doctrine of
non-intervention as being no solution and
failing altogether in duty. I put aside that of
conquest and aggrandisement, that of mercan-
tile tupidity,—namely, the opening of foreign
markets by force to British manufac-
tures, or to obtain violently, goods which
we could not otherwise get—as Wicked
and as hostile to the interest, and as' violating
the moral sense of civilised men. To construot
a policy suited in all respects to the compli-
cated position in which we are entangled,
would be a most diffioult task. To such a
work I make no pretension. Our comiection
with each separate country gives rise to many
political questions of the utmost difficulty,
vast social problems, deeply affecting the wel-
fare of millions of our fellow creatures. Look
at India, for example, with its young gentle- '
men rulers, who go out to get money, and to '
come home when they have got- it; where,
after our long rule, the British race fails now, as
it did at first, to amalgamate with the native
population; where we rule with ari arbitrary
despotic) sway, which we ourselves repudiate
altogether in pr
There is a great deal that we might do—and

and plainly before us. We have to reverse
our policy which has prevailed in the past.
We have not only to resolve to live a nobler
national life for the future, but we have also
to give the rest of the world assurance by our

policy of conquest, or aggrandisement, or

unredreised ; that no feeling of self-interest,
of national pride or vanity, shall hinder this.
from being done ; and that they shall at once
begin the work of constructing a Policy upon

THE CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT
ACT.

ANOTHER case of injustice and oppression
has been added to the unjustifiable convictions
which have taken place under this Act. It
appears that a Mr. HENRY GWYNNE, a general
engineer, carrying on business with his brother
at Hammersmith, had been petitioned by the
workmen in their employ, asking for the adop-
tion of the nine hours to commence on the tat
of January, which the Messrs. GWYNNE re-
fused to grant, and the men thereupon, to the
number of 103, gave a week's notice in writ-
ing of their intention to leave. They were
however, immediately paid off and looked out.
The men, as a matter of course, immediately
issued a notice that a lock-out had talon

place, and circulated the notice among their

fellow workmen, and, in 'order that Trades
Unionists may clearly understand ,what they
are liable to be indicted for, and convicted as
criminals, I append
,the circular in question,
which speaks for itself:--" Nine Hours Move-
ment.—January 6th, 1872.—Fellow workmen,
—We, the late workmen of the Hammersmith
Iron Works, having endeavoured to come to•
some arrangement with our employers, J. and
H. GWY:NNE, with respect, to the nine hours
movement to commence on the let of January,
1872, beg to inform you that we have failed in
this matter, and were locked out on the oat
and 14th, of December, 1871. We therefore
appeal to you, as fellow workmen, not to enter
into anyeugagement 'with our employers, unless
on the condition that the nine hours per day
commences
,at once. By so doing you will
forward our cause as well as your, own. It is
only by union that we, the working classes,
can rise to an elevation never yet attained.—
We remain, fellow workmen, yours truly,—The
Locked Out Men of the Hammersmith Iron
Works."

Now, it.. is
,impossible, to make a milder or
less offensive appeal or explanation by any
body of working men to their fellows, and
how in the world the magistrate could see any
thing bearing the semblance of " coercion
or intimidation" must be a matter of surprise
to 4 good. many people.
It is quite evident that the working men
have little or no .better .prospeat of obtaining
justide from the stipendiary, than they have
from the unpaid inag,istrates.
•Bat, in reality,
the fault lies with the Act which gives the
power to magistrates to put whatoverconstruc •
tion he ilk-coupon. the motives, a,Lts, andoruon-

stranees of working men, when any dis-
putes arise between them and their employers.
This is exactly what the framers of The Act
intended it should be, knowing well that as a
general rule those who administer the law,
look with a keen and suspicious eye "upon
working men in trade disputes.

The question was raised at the late Trades
Congress as to who were at fault for passing
this Act, some blaming the Tories and some
the sham Liberals. The fact is, they are both
at fault, and they must .both be reckoned with
at the proper. time. It cannot be denied that
a great number of members calling themselves
Liberals, either voted for the Lords' Amend-

ments or absented themselves, fearing the
consequences of their names appearing in the
division lists. On the other hand, a considerable
number of Tories mustered, under :the leader-
ship of Mr. Oxruonicii: llAnov, and voted for
the Lords', Amendments. We could expect
little else from the most of them, but as to
those slippery sham Liberals who promisodeo
much upon the hustings and performed so
little in the Senate, it is to be hoped they will
be reckoned with when the time comes. Mr.
JOHN KANE, of Darlington, proposed that the re-
peal of "The Criminal Law Amendment
,Art"
should be made a test to all candidates at the
next election, and the Trades Congress carried
this resolution unanimously, and every dele-
gate then' present: ought to do his utmost to
give praetical effect to that decision. Nothing
short of the total repeal of the Act will softie()
to place the, working men" of this country
upon the same footing before the ordinary law,
as all other bodies or associations of men. The
mistake has been that any legislation should
have taken place at all upon the matter in the
form of a penal enactment,
,‘ What was really
required was :that the . old Combination Laws
should be repealed, and trades unions be placed
upon the same footing as .the unione.of ,em-
ployers,
.or the associations of the professional,
the trading, or mercantile community. If an
.embezzlement takes place by any of the ofheera
.of these associations :the common law is
quite. capable of (lcaling with thorn just
as it would do with the officers of trades
unions. . Again, the law of assault or intimida-
tion is. quite dear, and unmistakeable,-
.and
where, trades unionists were proved to have
been guilty of this, the common, or ordinary
statute law, is quite strong enough to punish
ofTenoes of this kind. Where, then, is the
necessity for a special, penaleuttettueut against
working men? Why, there ieno need for any-
thing of the kind; and the sooner such a piece %
of unjust and oppressive ellss legislation as

The CritninulLaw Amendment Aor is erased

from the statute book, the better. Several of
the most respectable barristers of the day have
declared against the stringent character of this
Act, including Mr. HENRY and. Mr. Alan=

Cuoanos, Mr. IiAItILISM, Mr. LUDLOW, and

others; und Professor BEEsI,I7, who speaks

with no uncertain sound, condemns the Act,
not only as a piece of unjust legislation, but
also in a moral and philosophical point of view;
and, besides, there are
_several faithful friends

of the worlaug classes in Parliament, who ---ai;;

equally to it; and it is a pity they are
not more
o sed
repnpuomerous
there.
Per my own part,
speaking from an experieneo of more -thau
thirty years, I declare that I have never seen,
as a general rule, anything in the oondiket of
trades unionists that would justify the passilt-g
of an Act of this desoriptiou.

2

It is no use concealing the fact; the
object ot this Act is to prevent working men
offering any remonstrance, or giving any ex-
planation to their fellow-workmen when any
strike Or dispute takes place between them and
their employers. lut the Act permits any
amount of coaxing, cajoling, or wheedling of
working men on the part of employers when
they require them to supplant the men they
may be in dispute with. Is it not a fact
that, in all strikes that have assumed any pro-
portions, and lasted any time, the employers and
their agents have Used the most unscrupulous
means to allure men from their homesto take the
place of the men on strike? The fact is, their
agents have scoured the Whole country—aye,
and all Europe in the case of the Newcastle
strike—and picked up all the waifs and strays
they could laitheir hands on. In addition to
this, they have covered the walls of almost
every town in the kingdom with lying posters,
and circulated handbills by the thousand,
compared with which the circular of the men
of Ilataniersmith reads like a text from Scrip-
ture. And when they have thus Managed to
get a few of the rag-tag gathered together
under the falsest of pretences, and placed upon
their works, where they soon discover they
have been deceived, there is no remedy pro-
vided for those men under the provisions -of
this precious Act.
Let the working men, therefore, look well
to this, and insist upon its total and uncon-
ditional repeal. I attended the Congress at
Notlingliam More particularly to move a reso-
liition for its total repeal than for any other
purpose, except to urge upon the Congress the
necessity of returning as many properly
qualified working men as possible, to Parlia-
ment at the next election. Both these
resolutions were carried unanimously, and the
Congress of Trades Union representatives
stands pledged to give practical effect to both.
_ _

Therefore, trades unionists must huokle on
their armour and go forth to their work with
energy and resolution. It is much harder
work to get a bad law repealed then it is to
procure its enactment. The working men
must everywhere besiege their representatives
in Parliament to vote for the repeal of the
Act. But, above all, they must prepare in
time to send working men from their own
ranks to represent them in the House of Com-
mons, who really understand their wants and
requirements, and whose experience and fit-
ness will best enable them to defend and ad-
vocate the interests of labour, and assert the
right of ,working men being placed upon the
same level before the law of the land as the
rest of their fellow-countrymen.

articles.title: ALFRED A. WALTDIC
articles.text:
ALFRED A. WALTDIC

INFLUENCE OF THE PEOPLE ON IN-
TERNATIONAL POLICY.

AN excellent and most suggestive article in
your issue of last week, by HENRY CROMPTON,
on "International Policy" is well worth
special consideration by the working men of
Great Britain, not only because it points out a
growing popular fallacy, and stamps it as such,
and indicates at the same time their true line of
duty, but because it appeals to working men as
the true power by which the higher truth and
nobler duty shall take shape and life, and
become active in influencing the future policy
of the country. The doctrine of "non-inter-
vention," or peace at any price, as at present
advocated by its most ardent friends, does not
spring from any true principle in connexion
with the business of human life, and cannot,
therefore, be made the basis of a sound national
policy. It is not the result of a full considera-
tion of the requirements of human duty, but
rather a policy originating in fear, or in the
misgivings which have naturally arisen from
Rucce,sion of serious and dangerous blunders.
And it is in this way, beyond all doubt, it has
come to be an accepted doctrine with many of the
most humane and liberal politicians in Great
Britain. A very slight acquaintance with
the history of Europe, is sufficient to give a
strong seeming justification to the opinions of
those who advocate non-intervention as a
national policy for England, simply because
our chief losses and misfortunes, as a nation,
have originated in an officious intermeddling
.4he affairs of others, But it ought to he
borne id mind, that this intermothilingi was

prompted by prejudices and interests which
were sectional, rather than national, and
were in defence of institutions which are ,
being. gradually modified by time, and by the
action of more liberal convictions amongst the
people ; and that, therefor, it is not wise to
limit the influence and power of the new
spirit of the nation by dogmas which derive
their force from old blunders and:, crimes;
but that it should rather be our aim to dis-
cover the truest and soundest • principles of
national policy, and our duty to use our new
power, as a people, to embody them in our,
ordinary inter Course with the other natiOns of
the world.

The great war which siirang from the first
French Revolution, and. which before its ter-
mination, cost us so much, would not have been
possible, so far as we were concerned, had. the
general public mind. been as enlightened then'
as now, and had political power been as
general a possession amongst our people. A
class then held the power and resources, of the
nation in their control, and they used these
unscrupulously and profusely for the promo-
tion of class purposes, though certainly not
without some sort of underlying patriotic
intention. The last swar by which Europe was
disgraced, though not shared in by us, was not
a war of nations for great national objects—for
the conferring of benefits or blessings on the
masses of the people, but a contention between
crowned heads and plotting diplomatists; To
the honest workers in both countries it brought
only suffering and misery. From the commence-
ment of the world it may be said that this
game, with considerable variations, has been
played, and so long as class dominion is main-
tained it will most assuredly go on, and the
people will have to pay the cost. If this
state of things must be continued, if
class influences must predominate and class
interests override the interests of the public,
then by all moans let us bind. those who rule
us to their good behaviour by every possible
bond.; let us propound and enforce every
&gale-likely to have this effect without being
too nice as to its truth, or as to its fitness ,for
promoting the highest political duties. We
want peace; we require such conditions of
international policy as will enable us to pursue
. the civilizing and enriching operations of trade
with as few and brief interruptions as possible.
But English working men, having newly entered
into the possession of political power, should
ask themselves, without an unnecessary
moment's delay, whether they are now pressed
by a necessity so disheartening. What is to
prevent our working men from this time forth
determining, that in every right sense the
interests of the nation shall take rank before
those of class or sect. And, having so deter-
mined, should they not carry out their resolve
with an intelligent discrimination and a manly
vigour of purpose? If, in throwing them-
selves into the political conflict, they assert
old principles, follow old leaders, shout
old war cries they but increase the magni-
tude and confusion of the conflict, without
elevating its aims, or ennobling its spirit.
Whereas, it is their bounden and pressing
duty to act with definite intentions, and with
on unalterable determination to make every
personal and class pretension give way
for the purpose of scouring the inestimable
blessings of national and international justice.
Mr. CIIOM2TON says that International policy
"is not a game of skill, at which subtle
monarchs or wily well-read diplomatists spend
their lives, trying to cajole and circumvent
each other, in which they play with countries
and peoples, as they migp.t play with the
castles and pawns of a ganie of ohess." It is
true International policy ought to be some-
thing better and more elevated than this; but
only the people can make it so. In the interest
of the masses of the 'people, diplomatic
lies, feignings, shifts, and doubles are
of no earthly use, . as nothing can
permanently benefit them, unless it be
true in principle and just in prac-
tice'. A dynasty may be served by a politi-
cal• fraud. A class or a caste may gaiii an
important advant,i,ge byviolende and lid ustice ;
a family may strike lasting red in robbery;
but not so with a people. Starting from the
first begiunings of civilized society, the more a
sense ef justice has been difftisal, the more its

spirit has been embodied in the laws and
usages of society, the larger the gain in com-
fort and happiness, in liberty, security, and
content to the masses of the people. We
want, as .Mr. CROMPTON says, a code of Intern
national duty, in which politics shall be sub-
ordinated to Morals—that is we require Inter-
national understandings and policies resting
on honest mutual sympathies, sustained by
true. popular instincts, and. Etanotioned by that
universal popular consent, which in matters of
fair and honourable dealing, far transcends
the judgments of statesmen or philosophers.
All instahce of thisi alrnost unpleasantly con-
venient j ust now, is that afforded by our present
quarrel with America. If our working people
at the commencement of the late American
struggle eounted in the nation as an operating
and direct political force, the present unhappy
state of things could have had no existence.
Their honest desire to see liberty extended, to
see peace maintained, and the progress of
America, which was a blessing to them, con-
tinue uninterrupted, would have kept England
within the limits of her duty whilst that
struggle lasted; and consequently would have
rendered unnecessary .the compensations and
complications now scaring our "better classes
of people." But the working people then were
not a direct political force, and therefore
wore not of gauch account to the riding
elasses and. their friends, Our aristocracy
rejoioed in. the threatened breaking up of
America because she was a great suc-
cessful Republic. Our trading middle classes
were delighted at the misfortune of commercial
rivals, as a shabby shopkeeper might be
at the burning down of a successful com-
petitor's premises; whilst, our newspaper
men 'became insane iu their abuse, because it
is their interest to share in a Common knavery
or countenance a common folly, flow all this
class prejudice, hatred and jealousy can effect the
nation's safety ttud welfare, we are now begin-
ning to find out. To alter the state of things
alluded to hero, the working men have only to
enter actively on their, political duties. And
should they decide to do this, and put the
seal of an intelligent patriotism into their
work, they will very, soon discover a change
for the better in the nation's policy. Not non-
intervention, for that, after all is a policy of
cowardice, though it soothes our self-love to
call it prudence. Intervention to aid truth
against falsehood, to assist the right against
the wrong, or, the weak against the strong,
must always remain with us as an individual
and national duty. But this duty can only be
rightly performed when the peaceable indus-
trious masses of the several nations of Europe
bring their own sense ofjustice and right, and
their own appreciation of peace, of friendliness
in national intercourse, to bear on the polities
of the day; and, above all, when they show a
settled determination to subordinate aristo-
cratic pride, sacerdotal ambition, and commer-
cial greed, to those higher principles, of justice,
by which alone nations can thrive, and by
which only a true friendly national intercourse
can bo established and maintained.

LLOYD Jo NES.

FAR BETTER THAN £lO,OOO.

OF all the subjects 6 which the attention of
working men can be directed, beyond those
which relate to the providing for .their imme-
diate wants, and of course holding their
ground as far as they can against the tyranny
of capital while they are involved iu the com-
petitive system, they are none which in im-
portance can approach the question as to the
means by which they may deliver themselves,
as a class, from dependence upon the will and
pleasure of employers; from the uncertainties
of competitive commerce; from the fears of
future poverty for themselves and their fami-
lies; from the humiliation of being treated as
inferiors by their fellow men who are less
unfavourably placed; from the outrageous
injustice of being robbed of ti very large pro-
portion of the value of their work, as the
condition upon which alone they can obtain
permission to labour and to live, except as
paupers or as thieves; and from the injurious
institutions, arrangements, and practices, in
general, of the existing system.

A working man would think himself highly
fortunate if be were 0 reoeiye leguoy of

£lO,OOO ; and it is thought a great aohievement
if a man is so successful in his trade or pro-
fession as to realize a large fortune. But
there is far more in value, beyond comparison,
than any large fortune, however acquired, to
be obtained by every working man, and by
everyone, by the change of system which may
no* be realised. Everyone will obtain many
most important advantages by this change,
which even the millionaire, or the man of the
highest rank or position, cannot enjoy in, the
old system, and will b delivered from many
very serious disadvantages to which even
these highly-favoured individuals must inevi-
tably be subjected. For even these persons
cannot escape from the effects of the kind of
character which is acquired in this system, by
themselves, by their familie-s, and by their
fellow men in general—from the endless rami-
fications of evil consequent upon this character
and this system. And it is to be observed 4
that no one, who is in health, who does not
perform, or who has not performed, a fair pro-
portion of the work of society, except the
very young, can be living a really honourable
or honest life.

Here is a prize for the working classes to
strive for; and which not only a few, if sin-
gularly fortunate, and very clever, and very
cunning, and perhaps very unscrupulous, maY
gain, by finding means to appropriate
•the
results of the industry of others, but which all
may obtain by thoroughly honest and honour-
able means, highly conducive to the happiness
of all. And it is .a prize which no power on
earth can prevent their obtaining if they will
do what is necessary to obtain it—far less
than a man must do to make a fortune—and
if, as a necessary beginning, they will first
study the subject until they understand it,
and will then teach themselves, and help each
:other to acquire, the kind and the intelligently
considerate and just feelings which Will. be in
agreement with the new knowledge.
The great mistake which has been made by
social reformers in general, has been that of
,imagining that effectual social reforms can be
realised without this intellectual and moral
_reform in man himself--at first in those who
are tolls the leading agents in effecting the
required external changes. It is a very
natural mistake for those to make who are not
aware, except very superficially, of the course
of causation by which the evils of the

Population, of all classes, intellectually and
morally.; and who do not see that this charac-
ter is the eject of ignorance and erroneous
ideas respecting the causes of evil and of good to
man, especially in the formation of character;
and that this ignorance and these erroneous
ideas (forming together the primary cause cf
evil to man) must be superseded by the know-
ledge of these causes (which will be the primary
cause of good) before we can have the charaCter
which is the only basis upon which aaatisfee"

structed ; and who, therefore, have not theitt"
selves acquired this improved intellectual an•
fl
moral character. But there is no difficulty in

of the subject are clearly pointed out;
there will not be much difficulty for th°s°

influence of the new knowledge. It is oulY

And although they have seen the necessity for

and fatal defects of all the education of the old,

good, by whieh alone the right development 0L
man's moral nature can be produced.. In short',
they have not known the deeper %%uses of eV"
and of good to Man, peculiar

The only social reformer who has 'pointed
out the facts in which these causes are mani-
fested, is ROBERT OWEN, and we saw beauti-
fully exemplified the effects of this knowledge,
in his admirable qualities, in all the relations
of social life, and as a highly enlightened,
most kindly, gentle, generous, consistently
just, morally couregeous, •. and untiring
philanthropist, unswerving in his confidence
in the excellence Of 'man's43.ature, because he
knew, from his extensive and unique educa-
tional experience, arid felt in himself, what
man will be under favourable influences. And
these effects in this first example of the
influence of the new knowledge as a cause of
good in the formation of character, will be seen

by those who are able to appreciate them,

hs the idea "That man's character, and his

.causes and to deny this

The second (the idea "that man's character,

articles.text:
A FREE BREAKFAST TABLE.

MR. RIGBY WAsorr challenges your readers
to produce a plan by which an untaxed break-
fast table can be had within two years.
The sum annually set aside towards pay-
ment of the principal of the National Debt is
about two millions, and this would meet the
duty on tea.

Unfortunately the crotchet of paying off the
National Debt by means of belly taxes (more
iniquitous because more insidious than a poll
tax) this crotchet, I say, has unfortunately
met the support, not only of Mr. GLADSTONE
and Mr. LOWE, but also of Lord DERBY and
Mr. Dlsniumr.

If the Military Estimates were made out
according to the regulations and practice of
the Service (the law written and unwritten of
the army), they would be about four millions
per annum less than they now are.

The naval estimates would be about three
millions less, and the two together would equal
the taxes on sugar, coffee, and the remaining
articles belonging to the breakfast table.

There arc now fully twice as many officers in
the Array and Navy as the practice of the
service declares necessary. ,
According to the practice of the service, a
battalion of infantry should consist of from
1,200 to 1,500 men; by the " Cadet " system
now in use, the actual numbers are 500 to 600
men, the number of officers being in all cases
very nearly the same. The pay and pension
list is doubled in order to officer the army with
old fogies.

G. W. FIELD.

IMPROVIDENCE OF THE WORKING

CLASSES.

TIIE Earl of DEnnx presided over a very
crowded and influential meeting in the
Theatre of the Society of Arts, a few days
since, when Mr. G. C. T. BARTLEY' road a
paper on the duty of the working classes
making provision for old age. The paper eon-
tamed many good points, but especially was it
remarkable for dtiing justice to Trades Unions.
Perhaps never before had some of those pre-
sent beard so much of the " good side" of
Trades Unions. The speaker, with remarkable
boldness and clearness, pointed out the econo-
mical and prudential benefits t'esulting from
these Unions, above and beyond the question
of capital and wages, in the opinion of sonie,
the only object of these societies. But the most

atnentable thing in the whole affair was the

utter ignorance of those who aspired to instruct.
Some men think it their mission to lecture

working men on all kinds of subjects, and they
are so opinionated, and satisfied. that they
know all about it, that if a worker stands up
to speak for himself, they deem it presumption.
There were several men at the meeting above
referred to, who were able to instruct both
chairman and speakers if an opportunity had
boon given; but only one could get the oppor-
tunity of speaking, and he had to break the
rule laid down by the chairman that every
speaker should hand up his '',card." Not only
is it next to impossible for working men to gat
in a word at these meetings, but the middle
class Press never report them if they speak.
The reports of the next morning gave Earl
DERBY at length, surely not for the words of
wisdom he uttered on this occasion, but be-
cause he is the Earl of Maur. But of all the
pitiable exhibitions, that of Sir CHARLES
TREVIMYAN was the saddest. He appeared

like a boy who, believing he could swim,
plunged into a stream quite out of his depth,
where he kept floundering and splashing
deeper and deeper, until the audience, out of
sheer compassion, cheered him down. Poor
Sir tinntu.s could not at first see how pain-
fully he was struggling, and when he did per-
ceive it, the collapse was sudden, and no doubt,
to the orator, painful. Good intentions, Sir
CRADLES, is not the only qualification needed
'for dealing with these things.
Mr. DUDLEY BkXTER also got into a Scotch
mist, or surely he would never have stated
that one reason why working men do not put
money into the Post-Office Savings. Banks is
because, not being able to read and write, they •
tyre often plundered. It would be a remark-
able thing if, with the vast amounts annually
passing through these banks, not a single case
of dishonesty 4ecurred ; but everyone knows,
who has ever used the 13,05. J., that illunder

is next to impossible. We have never heard
of any case where the workmen refused to
fund their savings in consequence of plunder.
No, Air. DUDLEY BAXTER, such statements
add nothing towards a solution of the question
before us. Neither are the examples he quoted
from the Continent, unless all the exceptional
circumstances are fully given, and a fair com-
parison drawn in the two cases. The several
speakers stated that the causes of improvidence
were ignorance, neglect, and wastefulness, on
the part of our working population. To this
I replied that it was neither due to ignorance,
neglect, or wastefulness, but to inability.
Frankly confessing that there are those who
could save if they were more careful, I yet con-
tended that, taking the average of our working
population, it was impossible that anything like
a fair provision could be made for old age, and
for these reasons—First, lowness of wages. Is
it possible for agricultural labourers to save
out of is., Bs., Os., or 10s. per week? Can
dock labourers save out of 4d. per hour, espe-
cially with this drawback, that they sometimes
have to play four or five hours in the day?
Can the costermonger save 'Why, if some
of them got their goods for nothing, and
had all the proceeds of their sales as profit,
it would barely suffice for a living. There
are cabmen again, a numerous body of
men, and yet, so far as reliable evidence
goes, they cannot average more than from 15s.
to I.Bs. per week. To these provision for old
age is impossible. Their chief anxiety is to
get bread from day to day, and in the daily
struggle old age is scarcely hoped for. For
such as these, the utmost we can hope at
present is that they shall be able to get
healthier homes, better and cheaper food, and
obtain education for their children.

Going a btep higher, we find the day

labourer, in the' building trades, the iron
trades, railway porters, warehousemen,
policemen, carmen, and numerous others in

the great world of London, whose average
wages is scarcely over a guinea a week, even
if all the year round it amounts to so much.
What margin is there hero for the Payment
of a continuous sum weekly for 25 or 30
years. If they lay by something it is for
sickness, or out of work; and Heaven knows
the margin for such savings is small enough
131 All conscience.

But the editor of the .Echo—" preaohar of
sweetness and light" says- tho English
labourer is wasteful, he throws away the pods
of peas, whereas Frenchmen would stew them
down for a bountiful repast. Perhaps there is
no tangible reason why the English workmen
should not live on potato parings, leaving the
mealy morsel for his wealthier brother. The
noble chairman indeed said that the condition
of the labouring population was so hopeless that
they could not be expected to save for old age.
But he added, by way of corrective, that our
peasantry did not save like those of France,
Belgium, Holland, and other Continental
countries. Surely his lordship must know the
reason. The small farm system gives those
peasants some chance of saving. Every day's
labour can add something to the value and
productiveness of the land, and all this is
banking for the future.
If our agricultural labourers had but a plot
of land on which to bestow all their idle hours,
with awl security of tenure that the value
added to the land would be ever their own,
then England's •peasants would bear corn.
parison with all the world.

Lot us now turn to our artizans, and see how
far they could follow the advice of the speaker
above mentioned. Building operatives; me-
' °hanks in the engineering trade-3, printers,
cabinet trades, and a host of others get, say
from .E 1 16s. to £2 per week. If this were
constant, there can be no doubt they could
save something for the future. But lot
us see how the case stands. The em-
ployment of building operatives is, as a
rule, extremely precarious. Time is lost
on account of weather, waiting for materials,
change of employer, &0., Sie. Joiners who
work in the shop are kept on all the year
round, but their number is but a minority of
the trade. So precarious is employment in
the building trades, that, taking the last ten

years as a test, I question if the wages of the

wholi of the biddiiig trades Wouli literate

• 255. per week. This leaves but a small
margin for life assurance or annuities, espe-
cially after deducting is. per week for trades
or benefit societies' purposes.
Then there are engineers, ironfounderF p
iron ship builders, and numerous other trades
whose work is tolerably constant, but yet who
sometimes are out of employment very
many weeks together, thus reducing their
average wages. I question if the average
all through these trades would be more
than 275. or 28s. per week. The author
of the paper stated that young men who
commenced paying is. 11d. per week
at 20, and continued paying until 55, would
be entitled to 103. per week for the remainder
of their lives; or if he commenced at 25,
by paying 2s. sd. per week, he would realise
the same annuity at 55. It scorns never to
have entered into the head of the writer, that
such continuous payment, in addition to other
similar payment to trades, benefit and other
societies, must moan continuous employment,
at good wages, for thirty years. And who,
that has any knowledge of working class life,
can be ignorant of the fact that this falls to
the lot of but few, oven amongst the best paid
artizans.
' Such dreamy speculations on unreliable
data is useless. There is, indeed, one way in
which such provision could be made, viz.,
let the eleven millions and a half sterling,
now paid to the poor rate—a compulsory tax,
which all must pay, and from which we dare
not seek relief except under the brand
of pauper—be paid over• to a wealthy
insurance company, and they, ens merely com-
mercial priuoiple, would keep all our pour, not
from starvation only, but in comparative com-
fort; they would provide for sickness, out of
work, accident, death, and old age; and, no
pauper's brand would be the result of an ap-
plieation for the benefits for which they were
insured; but manly independence would be
developed, which would never stoop to fraud.
If our sage legislators arc unable to supply the
necessary solution, as the noble chairman
admitted himself to be, let the work be handed
over to a commercial company under proper
Government supervision, and they would soon
find the capital for all such purposes. Only
fancy an annual income of £11,500,000 ster-
ling, mostly paid in advance. Why poverty
would absolutely disappear. It is next to

impossible to caleulate the result of the appli-
oation of such an annual revenue if in the
hands of business men, but the Poor Law
Board bas.shown its incapacity to comprehend
and deal with pauperism, mostly created by
the very State which has to apply the remedy.

There is another useful work which the
Government might undertake profitably, and
with the most beneficent results to working
men, namely, National Building Societies in
connotation with the Post Office Savings Bank.
These societies could, place within the reach
of all, the means to acquire a house and plot
cf land at even less cost than is now paid fur

two rooms in our crowded. cities. The Govern-
ment is now lending money, repayable at £5
is. per cent, per annum, principal and interest,
so that a loan of £3OO could be obtained at the
rate of £l5 3s. per year. There was lent
£15,000 not long since to a wealthy company
in Loudon to provide better homes for working
men, but the company got a handsome per-
centage on the capital thus provided. Why
not lend money to poor men to buy their own
homes, and thus give them some practical
interest in the welfare of the land of their
birth? Earl DEncY thought he made quite a
hit at social innovators when he said that

hose who wore noisy demagogues and thom.

who were led by such leaders bad nothing- to
lose. This is what we say and would have it
altered. There is much to be done, my Lord

DEneY, before working meu can afforci to keep
up a continuous payment of 2s. per week fur
annuities. We must induce theta to live in

botar homes, taking care that these are pro-
vided, see to it that these homes are well and

comfortably furnished, get wholcsotue food and
reasonably decen.t clothing, with such little

provision for sickness awl out of work as our
best soeieties provide; and a considerable portion
._ _

of this to ybil difficult problem, will be 'solved.
The tneu have all their work to do to keep
straight from month to mouth, arid arisout4trit

4

if rent can be paid, and food :obtained for
themselves and their families.
Tens of thousands of our best skilled artizans
look to no higher life than plenty of work,
fair wages, and reasonable hours. To have a
couple of rooms, one for living, one for sleeping,
fair food, and the chance of a holiday once or
twice a year without being pinched for the cost,
iS no very extravagant demand, and yet, if
but this could be obtained, our artizans and
labourers would continue to keep the lead in
all the markets of the world.

Some of our statisticians like LEONI LEVI,
or DUDLEY BAXTER are startled at the enormous
sum paid. to the toiling population in the shape
of wages, the highest of which they put at
£418,000,000 sterling.
Yet this vast sum has to be divided
amongst 11,000,000 of toilers and bread
earners; so that after all, it only just amounts
to £3B per annum, and this has to keep the
whole of the families, as well as the toilers,
of our country. Here then we have, say, an
average of 14s. Od. per week for the total of our
industrial population, and yet these men talk
of saving and laying by 2s. per week for
annuities in old age. It is simply monstrous.
We shall, ere long, have to bestir ourselves
in the matter of our enormous poor rates, and
ts(e to it that the eleven and a half millions
sterling are applied to the object for which
they are imposed, viz., the sustenance of our
toiling poor, or, if not, an Anti-Poor-Rate
League must be formed to resist further pay-
mente for a merely pauper's dole.

To the Editor of tho BEE-HIVE.

SIR,—As there is now an overwhelming voice
being raised by the working men of the country
in all trades for reform, will you give the men of
the Thames a space in your columns, to enable
them to show your readers and the Legislature
what is tho reform they require? Briefiy this
that, as at present constituted, they are bontrolled
by, a self-elected board, all employers, who are,
so to speak, the self-elected executive committee
of a legal trades union, under the title of the
Watermen and Lightermen's Company, with
powers, by Aot of Parliament, of compelling
every member to pay an annual subscription,
beside other fees, to the extent of £4,000, beside
other sources of income, amounting, in the total,
averaging £7,000 per annum, as shown by the
balance-sheet enclosed; and none of its members
until over sixty years of age participate in its
benefits, and that commencing with the paltry suni
of £2 ranging to £lO per annum ; and the officials
have admitted, before a Committee of the House
of Commons, having now 500 applicants still for
pensions.:The other charities are forty alms-houses
at Penge, and other trust property, all under the
same management. Now, the question may be
Asked, what reform is it that the niombers of this
Association (or Company) require? Why, sir,
this, as in all other societies, associations, &c., that
every paying member over 7,000 shall have the
privilege of voting into• office the governing
committee; so that, instead of its:costing, as it
does now; as per balance-sheet, £1,455 9s. 9d. to
keep the power in the hands of the self-elective com-
mittee, offiaers' salaries, and office expenses, which
is the average cost to administer the poor funds,
&c., for the officers do not do only nominally their
other duties ; the account will show that less than
£2,000 is given to the poor members; while the
expenses is the above'eaormous sum. I therefore
ask you to assist the hard working oppressed men
of the Thames, to bring this question before the
Friendly Societies Commission, so that we may
show to the Commission what it costs to dole out
the miserable pittance tO the poor and aged
members. In conclueion, I ask, are we not
justified in asking for representation when we are
compelled to pay taxation?--I am, Sir, yours
most. respectfully,

TIIE IRON TRADES.

The West of Scotland Iron Trade Short- time
League are also agitating for a reduction of
working hours to 51 per week, without a corres-
ponding reduction of wages. The masters have
offered 54 hours. So far, there is no prospect of a
settlement of the dispute.

articles.title: TEE CABINET MAKERS.
articles.text:
TEE CABINET MAKERS.

A partial strike of tho cabinet makers and
upholsterers of Glasgow has. commenced, and
already 500 or 600 men have left their employ-
ment. The men asked for a reduction from 57 to
52 hours per week, without any corresponding
reduction of wages, and that overtime should be
paid at the rate of time and a quarter. T,he
Masters' Association offered 64 hours; but this,
like a subsequent prOposal to refer the question to
arbitration, was refused, and the masters, with a
few exceptions, have determined on a lock-out.

articles.title: TYNE. THE SUIP CARPENTERS.
articles.text:
THE TYNE.
THE SUIP CARPENTERS.

The ship carpenters of the Tyne have given a
fortnight's notice of their intention to ask an
advance of wages from ss. to 6s. a day. The
house carpenters and joiners of North and South
Shields have also notices in for higher wages and
shorter hours.

articles.title: DURHAM. THE COLLIERS.
articles.text:
DURHAM.
THE COLLIERS.

The pitmon of the county of Durham still con-
tinue to hold meetings for the purpose of sustain-
ing the agitation for the abolition of the yearly
bond in March. The question, however, is not
likely to cause any complications, as it is under-
stood that the colliery owners are:willing to sub-
stitute fortnightly agreements for the bond.
Another advance of 7 per cont. was made last
week in most of the Hornhold collieries, in the
Durham district, on the hewers' wages.

articles.title: SOUTH STAFFORDSHIRE.
articles.text:
SOUTH STAFFORDSHIRE.

MEETING Or THE MEN.

On Monday morning, a large meetiug of all
classes of ironworkers—delegates and workmen—
was held at Great Bridge, near Dudley, to consider
the proposition put forth by the masters at
the last Conference at Wolverhampton. The
Chairman explained to the meeting that there
were two courses open to them. The first was to
decide whether they would go up and down with
the price of iron is. in advance of the poundage,
or whether they would accept the masters' offer of
lie. 6d. for puddling, as the maximum, and Bs. 6d.
for puddling as tho minimum. Both propositions
found favour with sections of the men for some
time, but the feeling wore gradually round in
favour of a sliding scale proposed by the men. ,It
was explained by the chairman and others that
whatever resolution the men came to that day,
the masters would give the men an immediate
advance of is. per ton.
It was then almost unanimously agreed that
the men should return to work at the profferred
advance until June, and after that time they
should rise and fall with the price of iron.
Previous to the decision, three delegates from
North Staffordshire and Darlington addressed the
men in favour of founding a new association, and
the men agreed to take the necessary steps.

articles.text:
SOUTH WALES.

THE STEAM COAL ARBITRATION.

We are enabled this week to chronicle the
Successful termination of the Cardiff Arbitration,
Which has been natulally looked forward to with a
good deal of anxiety. It may, indeed, be said with
propriety that the Arbitratiop, proper never com-
menced, for a complete agreement was come to
between the contending parties on the points which
were ot issue without the necessity of hearing the
very elaborate evidence which would otherwise
have been indispensable, or of calling for the in-
terference of the Umpire. The decision arrived
at seems to give satisfaction to all, and we may
trust that the provisions agreed to for the peace-
able settlement of Jam) disputes will secure for
the Welsh Steam coal trade a lengthened period of
uninterrupted industry.

The following are the terms agreed to by the
representatives of both parties:—" The arbitration
workmen to be paid an advance of 21 per cent.
Upon the rates paid in May, 1871, for wages from
August 20th, 1871, to February 20th, 1872. That
taking it as admitted that an advance of 10 per
cent. upon the now existing rates of wages is
about to be made by the proprietors oft be iron-
Works in the neighbouring ,districts, the arbitra-
tion proprietors will make stroll a further advance
in wages as will make the rates payable in their
works 12i per cent. higher than those paid there
In May, 1871; this further advance to take effect
front February 21st, 1872, it being understood that
Any further rise or fall that shall take place in the
ironworks of Monmouthshire and South Wales
Subsequently to the 10'per cent. now contemplated
Shall regulate any Aubsoquent rise or fall that shall
be made in the arbitration works; but that no rise
Or fall in wages payable to colliers in particular
il'anworks, independently of any general rise or fall,
shall affect the wages that shall be payable in the
arbitration works. It is further agreed that in ease
any differences may arise upon the award they be
referred to Mr. Macnamara, or, failing him, to some
referee to be natned by the parties, or, if they can-
not agree, to a referee to be named by one of the
Judges of her Majesty's superior courts. Dated
Ist February, 1872." Subsequently the masters
agreed that the entire 121 percent. advance should
commence from Ist February, and offered to give
21 per cent. for the past six- months if the men
Would do the same to form the nucleus of an
lusurance fund against colliery accidents.

MASS MEETING OF COLLIRIIB.

On Friday evening the colliers mustered. in
largo numbers at the Temperance-hall, Abordam,
for the purpose of hearing addresses from Mr.
Alexander M(Donald and Mr. T. Halliday bearing
PM the late gratifying adjustment of disputes be-
tween the employers and their workpeople.
•E'llortly before seven o'clock, the appointed

hour for the commencement of the meeting, Mr.
M`Donald and Mr. Thomas Halliday entered the
hall, and, in making their way to the platform,
received great cheering from the persons assem-
bled. The vast building was crowded.
With but one isolated exception, the men at
various stages throughout the proceedings testified
their accordance and warm appreciation of the
arrangements secured in their behalf, and re-
echoed by a loud and ringing cheer the sentiments
of their friends, when acknowledging the good
feeling evinced by the employers towards the men
throughout the conduct of proceedings at Cardiff.
The genuineness of expression could not be for
a moment doubted, and the only point which yet
remains unsettled is one in which the men only
can have an intense interest, and after the generous
offer of the masters with respect to the establish-
ment of a provident fund, we opine that sober-
thinking men, who have the smallest amount of
regard for their own welfare and that of their
fellows, will require little persuasion to induce a
ready acceptance of this benevolent proposal.
After the addresses, it was proposed seconded,
and carried that the terms set forth in the award
be accepted.

It was then proposed, seconded and carried, amid
much cheering, "That the best thanks of this
meeting be given to the employers for tho interest
they had shown in bringing the late dispute to a
close, and all others connected with the adjust-
ment."

A vote of thanks to the arbitrators was ac-
knowledged, and the mooting terminated.

VIE MINERS 'AI) TUE IRON WORICERS.

A .qonference of mine-owners .and miners on the
dispute es to the demand for the.nine hours system
was held at Stoks-on•Trent on Friday afternoon.
Mr. T. P. Twomlow, chairman of the Stafford-
shire Quarter Sessions, presided, at the request of
both sides. The case put forward by the Men was

that the state of trade warranted them in seeking
an improvement in their position, either in the
shape of *increased wages or reduced hours of
work; that the present hours are too long, and
that the mental and moral condition of the miner
regaires raising. On the other hand, it NI as
alleged that but a. tsraall proportion of the men
were taking part in the movement, that a majority
of them were now working not more than nine

hours a day from their own disinclination to work
more; that the proposed reduction of hours would
be a disadvantage to many of the men, a loss to
the masters, would compel an immediate rise in
the price of coal, and would probably lead to a
further reduction of hours. After a long discus-
sion the masters promised to take the subject into
careful consideration without delay, and, in reply
to the men, agreed to refer the dispute to arbitra-
tion in the event of the parties being unable to
arrive at a settlement.

On the same day a deputation from the iron-
workers waited upon the irontntu3ters of North
Staffordshire in reference to the demand for an ad-
vance of wages. The masters offered to accept the
new scale to be adopted in South Staffordshire,
and the deputation promised to lay this proposal
before the general body of workmen.
The cOalowners of North Staffordshire held a
meeting on Monday, at tho Railway Hotel, Stoke,
to consider the claim of the colliers to have the
hours of labour reduced. It was resolved that the
working hours should be reduced to 62 per week,
with a proportionate advance of the rates to those
working by tonnage, scorago, or measure; or the
employers are willing to leave the working hours
as at present, and to pay an advance of 10 per
cent. in wages. Either arrangement to come into
operation as soon as accepted, and to be binding
on both sides up to the 30th Juno next. If
neither proposal be accepted the whole matter to
be submitted to arbitration. When this resolu-
tion had been passed a deputation of colliers at-
tended, and after some discussion it was resolved
that if the workmen accepted the first part of the
foregoing resolution as a settlement to the 30th
Jena next, altering the weekly number of hours
from 52 to 50, the employers would assent to stich
alteration. At a meeting of 3,000 colliers held at
Hanley on Monday evening it was resolved to
accept the 50 hours till the end of June.

porters on the London district of the Great
Western Railway commenced an agitation for the
reduction of their period of labour to fifty-four
hours par week—Sunday to be paid for as over-

were presented to the Board of Directors, but no

It was resolved that a deputation consisting of six
delegates should wait upon the directors to ascer-
tain whether they wore disposed to make any, and
if 'so, what concession to the men, in compliance
with their former memorials.

Mast where fan blast is used, and 6d. per week for
carrying breezes."
Tho following document, the speaker said, had
been issued for the men to sign when engaged by
the employers, which he characterised as a most
tyrannical thing, and said the first man who was
asked to sign it refused :7--" I hereby agree to
work for you at the prices, and to observe the
rules of the 'Bolt, Nut, Rivet, and Railway
Fastening Manufactories Association,' which
prices and rules are sot forth in the price list which
is now posted at your works: and I declare that I
am not a member of the 'Nut and Bolt Makers'
Protection and Death Society of Darlaston, Smeth-
wick, and District;' and that I am not a member
of any other society or union of bolt and nut
makers, and that I will not become a member of,
or join, any such society or union as long as I re-
main in your. employ."

The Council were unanimous in their con-
demnation of this proceeding on the part of the
employers, and they resolved, on the' motion of
Mr. King, seconded by Mr. Plaskett, "That this
Council, having heard tho deputation, is of opinion
that their case is deserving of the support of the
trades of this locality, and that the credentials of
this Council be given them to enable them to
appeal to the various societies for support."
Mr GiMyer (secretary) gave notice that ho
should move at the next meeting, as the time was
then too far advanced,—" That in the opinion of
this meeting it is the duty of the Town Council to
adopt that part of the report of the Free
Libraries Committee which recommends the open-
4.ng of the Art Gallery and Reference Library
during some part of Sundays; that such a place of
resort would he of great value and much ap-
predated by a large number of the ',inhabitants of
this borough; and that, instead of lowering the
morality of those who may incline to visit that
institution during such times, it would tend to
encourage that study and that thought, and would
elevate the mind, raising them to the consideration
of higher subjects."

The Chairman gave notice that ho should move
a resolution at the next meeting, as to the desira-
bility of appointing a deputation to wait upon the
borough members to ask them to vote for the re-
peal of the Criminal Law Amendment Act.

articles.title: DUNDEE.
articles.text:
DUNDEE.

ArITTATION FOR A NINII nouns' FACTORY ACT.

A meeting of delegates representing the opera-
tives in the various factories in Dundee was
held on Monday evening, at which it was
agreed to support the English movement
for fifty-four hours. The feeling of the meet-
ing seemed to be in favour of . waiting the
result of the movement in England, and then to
agitate for adoption of the fifty-one hours system
in Scotland. Letters were read from Mr. Mundella,
Sir John Ogilvy, and Mr. Armistead,' M.P., and
from the Secretary of Factory Acts Reform Asso.
ciation, Bradford.

Mr. Mundolla, in his letter to the Secretary to
the Dundee delegates, said, "The Bill you refer
to is not in such a tante of forwardnesk as will
enable no to make any public statement respecting
it. This much, however, you may itely upon.
Any Bill I introduce will apply to the whole
factories and workshops of the three kingdoms,
and not exclusively to the cotton and woollen
mills. I consider a fifty-one hour agitation, in the
present state of the European labour market
unadvisable, and, believe me, it would prove
injurious to British industry. Be content with
fifty-four, and be assured it will be an easy task to
carry it."

LEEDS.

spinning, felting, and woollenraanufacturing trades
of Leeds, took place on Tuesday night, in the
British Workman Central Hall, for the purpose of
tonsidering what steps should he taken to obtain
the nine hours system. It was agreed that a cir-

articles.title: NORTHAMPTON. TILE NINE MUM' MOVEMENT.
articles.text:
NORTHAMPTON.
TILE NINE MUM' MOVEMENT.

The trades of Northampton held a mass meeting
on Wednesday evening at the Town-hall, which
was crowded, for the purpose of advocating the
establishment of the nine hours in that town.
The chair was occupied by the ex-Mayor' P. P.
Perry, Esq., J.P. ;.and upon the platform were
the members of the Trades' Council, the represen-
tatives of the various trade; and several influen-
tial gentlemen of the town.
The chairmau opened the proceedings in a short
but suitable and expressive speech, in which he
acknowledged his sincere and earnest sympathy
with working men in all their lawful efforts to im-
prove their condition.
Mr. George Potter then delivered an address on
the Relations of Capital and Labour and the Nine
Hours' Movement, which was listened. to with
great interest, and received with much satisfac-
tion.

Mr. Tompkins, carpenter, and Mr. W. Rice
seconded the following resolution :

Resolved,—" That in the opinion of this meet-
ing it is the duty of every working man to aid any
movement which has for its object the .shortening
of hours of labour' believing that it will pro-
mote the moral, intellectual and social advance-
ment of the people, and will further be useful to
the country by
.providing work for tho uneru-
Noyed."
Carried unanimously.
Mr. E. Brirnley moved, and Mr. E. Green
seconded the folloiving resolution :
" That this meeting rejoices in the establishment
of the nine hours as a day's work throtighout the
country, and hopes that the employers of 'North-
ampton will not refuse when asked to concede it,
for the benefit of their workmen,"
Carried by acclamation.

On the motion of Mr. Hammond, shoemaker,
hearty votes of thanks
.were given to Mr. G. Potter
and the chairman, after which the meeting termi-
nated.

• SHEFFIELD.
T/IX STRIKE AT THR DON WORKS.

At the Sheffield Town Hall, on Wednesday,
before the stipendiary magistrate, fifty-five men
appeared in answer to summonses taken out against
thorn by their employers, Messrs. Vickers, Sons,
and. Co., of the Don Works, Sheffield, for neglect
of work and for a breach of contr act. Mr. Barker,
barrister, appeared in support of the informations ;
and, Mr. ,Blackburn had boon retained for the
defence. The first case taken was that against
William Range, and it was to soma extent a teat
case. It appearedthat, on the morning of the 31st
of January, when the turners and fitters went to
their work, they found a young man working at a
steam lathe who had notserved the full term of hid
apprenticeship, and who was, in fact, an unskilled
labourer, When the foreman entered the shop he
asked the men why they were not commencing
work. They told him that they did not feel justi-
fied in working with an unskilled man, and called
upon him to remove him. The foreman said he could
not do. so without Mr. Vickers' permission, and
the men left the works in a body. When Mr.
Vickers arrived, a deputation from the men
waited upon him, but he refused to discuss the
matter with them while they remained on strike,
but would do so if they would resume work. But
that the men refused to do, and the whole of them
were summoned. The defence was that the men
considered they had a grievance ill having an
unskilled workman amongst them. they com-
plained to the foreman, but he refused to remove
the man, and told them that if they were not
satisfied they could go. The men interpreted these
words as tantamount to a dismissal and left. The
foreman denied that he used the words the on
alleged that he did. The stipendiary expressed no
opinion with regard to the men's refusing to work,
but held that the words of the foreman, even if he
did use them, did not amount to a dismissal. ge
therefore ordered the defendant to enter into his
own recognisances in S 5, and to find a surety in a
like sum, to return to bis work and fulfil his con-
tract. Mr. Barker, on the part of Messrs. Vickers,
said if the other defendants would return to their
work the whole of the other summonses would be
withdrawn. Mr. Blackburn, on the part or the
men, undertook that they should resume work
the next day, and the summonses were thereupon
withdrawn, .

MISCELLANEOUS TRADES NEWS.
EIIMINGHAIE.—A. general meeting of saddlers
and harness makers was held on Monday night at
the Acorn Inn, Navigation street, Birmingham.
It was unanimously resolved that the masters be

petitioned for an advance upon the present rate of
wages—viz., 15 per cont. upon all day workers,
and 15 per cont. on all piece work, and all neces-
sary materials found. Also for a reduction in the
hours of labour to 56 hours per week, each shop to
make the necessary arrangements with the em-
ployers. It was also resolved that the masters be
allowed until the Ist of March to consider their
decision, and that the increase of wages and de-
crease of work date from the 18t of April. A
committee, consisting of workmen of Birmingham
and Walsall, were appeinted to carry out the
arrangements for memorialising the masters.
WOLVERHAMI'TON.--.-011 Sunday evening a meet-
ing of railway servants was held at the Gladstone
Inn, North-road, Wolverhampton, for the purpose
of formingta ,branch association of the .Arnalga-
mated Society of Railway Servants, and for the
purpose of securing a different system of payments,
and a decrease in the hours of labour. It was
resolved to address a letter to the Great Western
Railway directors, setting] forth the men's griev-
ances, and requesting a reply by the 18th inst.
A. resolution was also passed, by which it was
decided to form a branch; of the Amalgitmated
Society of Railway Servants.

On Motley night, a meeting of lock and key
makers was held at the Golden Fleece Inn, Union-
street, Wolverhampton, Mr. J. Smith presiding.
It was statedfthat the masters had decided to give
the advance on theist of March. The chairman, in
an appropriate speech, urged the men to go to work
at ORO, and ultimately it. was resolved, on the
motion of Mr, Smith, seconded by Mr. Francis
Morris, "That ths, operative lock and key makers
hero assembled do hereby agree to accept the
masters' terms as proposed in...reference to the ten
per cent."
BRISTOL. TllO 113ristol journeymen bakers
struck:on Saturday for reduced hours and higher
wages.

NEwprELD,-31essrg. Bolckow, Vaughan, and
Co., in answer to a requisition,from the men, have
conceded an advance of 3d. per ton upon the
prices to the whole of the coke drawers employed
at their extensive eeke ovens at Newfield Colliery.

•
BARNBLEY.—Tho bleachers of Barnsley and the
district, Messrs. jackson and Co., Messrs. Craik,
Messrs. Spencer and Co., and Messrs. Carr, have
agreed to advance the wages of their men 5 per
cent., and reduce the hours of labour to nine per
day.

LANCASUIRE. *-- The East:liiding police are
petitioning for increased pay, on the ground of
dearness of provisions and the general advance in
the coat of living.
WEDNESBURY.—On Saturday evening a meeting
of colliery, mill, forge, and brick-kiln engine.
drivers, was hold at the Dartmouth Hotel, Wed-
nesbury, with reference to the nine hours move-
ment. Delegates attended...from; Wolverhampton,
.13ilston, Old Hill, Stourbridge, and other places.
After some discussion, it was agreed that another
memorial should be drawn vp on behalf of the,
whole of the engine-drivers of the district, and
presented to the employers at an early date.
WALSALL.—Mr. Elijah, Stanley, bridle-cutter,
&c., having conceded the nine hours system to his
workmen, they entertained him to supper in the
club room of the Temperance Hall, Walsall, on
Saturday evening last. Mr Stanley has intimated
to his piece hands that he is willing to give them
whatever advance the other employers decide upon.
BLAENIVON.—The collien' strike at Blaenavon,
which at one time assumed a very serieus aspect,
has been amicably settled. The company have
agreed to give an advance of wages in a fortnight,
and the men have resumed work.

Lord G. Hamilton, M.P., on Wednesday
presided over a-meeting of representatives of
metropolitan parishes affected by the Turn-
pike Abolition Act of last session, at which it
was resolved that measures should be taken
for the maintenance of the roads without
throwing the cost upon the several parishes,
and that a county rate would be the most
desirable means of supplying the deficiency.

The Convocation of the Province of Canter-
bury assembled at Westminster on Wednes-
day for the despatch of business. In the
Upper House addresses of congratulations to
the Queen and the Princess of Wales, on the
recovery, of the Heir-Apparent, were moved
by the Bishop of Winchester, seconded by
the Bishop of St. David's, and. carried. The
Lower House formally recorded its sympathy
with the Church on the loss of Bishop Patteson
and his companions in martyrdom.

Several paokages of diamonds arrived from
the Cape on Wednesday in the mail steamer.
The yield in the colony still continues to be
large. At the fields the diggers had taken the
law into their own hands, and burnt down
some canteens, the proprietors of which were
accused of purchasing stolen, diamonds from
the natives.

lIIPERTAL PARLIA.MENT.

THE QUEEN'S SPEECH.

The Imperial Parliament was formerly
opened on Tuesday by Royal Commission.
The event was diminished in interest by the
absence oilier Majesty. There was but little
excitement in the vicinity of Westminster.
In the House of Lords, the Peers appointed
to represent her Majesty, took their seats on a
bench in front of the Throne at two o'clock,
The Members of the House of Common"
having appeared at the Bar, with the Speeko
at their head,
The Lord. Chancellor read the following .

able.
I.am able also to congratulate 'von, .so far 0

dications, which are corroborated by a decline

un-
provement of Public Education in Scotland,

ment of what is known. as the Licensing PP-

Several measures of administrative improve-

You, my Lords and Gentlemen, will, I am

THE DEBA/ES ON THE ADDRESS.
HOUSE OF LORDS.

When the House of Lords reassembled at
five o'clock, there was a fair nnmber of peers
present.
The Address' which was as usual an echo
of the Royal Speech, was moved by Earl
Delawarr, and seconded by Viscount Powers-
court.
The Duke of Richmond, Earl Granville, and
Lord Derby took part in the short debate
which followed. The discussion turned mainly
'upon the Alabama question, and all these noble
lords agreed that there was no foundation or
justification for the claims recently put for-
ward by the United States. The Address was
adopted without a division.

Half an hour was taken upslay the "Notices
of Motion," which were between 50 and 60 in
number.
Mr. Gladstone gave notice that on Thursday
he will move for the appointment of a Com-

cutors ; Sir M. Lopes, on the 27th, will move

Contra

nounced his intention of asking Sir C. Mike

Royal Speech, was moved by

hoped, however; that the difficulty would only

and able speech the greater part of which was
devoted to 'preying the solindnesS of the
Prosperity of the country. He regretted the
miseeneeptinn in regard to the Geneva Arbi-
Yation, expressed a 4eoided opinion that the
ilefnis,ing system must be dealt with, and, as a

some -parts of the 'recent legislation on the

Mr. Disraeli commenced brui3marking that
since the last Session time had Passed more

Usual and convenient veil of oblivion over

tributed to the new habit Of the Ministry of

Judging, however, from the notices of motion
just given, Mr. Disraeli anticipated_ that the
Ministers would have ample . and.
.speedy
opportunities or defending themselves, in the

, Admiralty management 'and the , evasion 'Of

WORKING MEN'S COMMITTEE
FOR PROMOT I NG TUE

SEPARATION OF CHURCH AND STATE.

TO THE WORKING CLASSES OP GREAT BRITAIN.

FELLOW WORK M EN,—
The Working Men's Committee has been formed
in consequence of a prevalent imprcasion that
the time is come when the question of Separa-
tion of Church and State must be referred to the
final judgment of the people. In the last Session
of Parliament, it was submitted by Mr. Mall to
the judgment of the House of Commons. In

doing this, he had no expectation of immediate

success. As, however, an Act of Parliament had
separated the Church from the State in Ireland, he
felt himself warranted in asking the Legislature to
apply the principle of that measure to the rest of
the United Kingdom. He was met with the objec-
tion that the ease of Ireland was peculiar—which
indeed it was circumstantially, but not substan-
tially. Nevertheless, the Government which had
undertaken the disendowment and disestablishment
of the State-Church in Ireland, did not oppose tho
motion upon its merits, but attempted to show that
the question was not yet ripe for legislative action.
Mr. Gladstone closed his speech by suggesting to
Mr. Midi, that he must first convince a majority
of the people of the wisdom and justice of his
policy, before expecting Parliament to adopt it.
This unequivocal challenge of the Premier has

been accepted ; and the Society for the Liberation
of Religion from State-Patronage and Control has
determined to appeal to the people for an expres-
sion of opinion on the subject. The Working Men
of Great Britain have never yet, as a body, pro-
nounced any judgment on this great question; but
it has been felt that, after the broad challenge thrown
down by the Premier, they can no longer, with
respect either to him or to themselves, refrain from
a declaration of their honest and deliberate senti-
ments: From Mr. Miall, and the groat party that
he has formed in the country, Mr. Gladstone, as
loader of the Liberal party in the House of Com-
mons, and also as first Minister of the Crown, has,
in set terms, appealed to the People. It behoves
Working Men, therefore, to answer that appeal;
and that, not simply upon the purely numerical
ground suggested byMr. Gladstone, as to whether,
among the adult population of this Island, the
majority are in favour of, or against, the Dis-
endowment and Disestablishment of the State-
Church in Britain, as in Ireland, but also,
and perhapi especially, with a view to the
return of pledged candidates at the next
General Election, whensoever that may take
place. The House of Commons, as now consti-
tuted, does not embody a faithful and com-
plete representation' of the whole people; and,
without taking a pOll of the whole population, the
only means of answering the challenge OT the Pre-
mier consista.in the election of a House of Commons,
each member of which has been returned with a
special view to his avowed opinion on the groat
question thus gravely put to the issue.
These, then, are the circumstances under which
the Working Men's Committee for promoting the
Separation of Church and State has been formed,
and now proceeds to work.
The views of the Committee may be thus con-
sisely stated— _ _

1. They regard matters of religion as belonging
to the domain of conscience, in which everything
must be left between man and his Maker.

2. They arc of opinion that, slime the State
Church in one part of the United Kingdom has
been disestablishecl, it is both unjust and incon-
sistent not to deal in a similar manner with the
State-Churches of the other parts of the United
Kingdom
3. They are persuaded from observation and
experience, that the State-Church has utterly
failed to accomplish the task for which it was
established; and arc also convinced that its
existence, as such, is a fatal hindrance to the
attainment of those objects which churches of any
kind profess to keep in view.
4. The State-Church of England has failed as
manifestly as the State-Church in Ireland; the
only difference being, that, while the bulk of the
Irish People were Roman Catholics, in contradis-

tinction to the avowed Protestantisn of the then
State-Churoh, the great majority of the British
People are either members of the different Pro-
testant Nonconformist Churches, or of the Church
of Rome, or are willing to remain of no Church,
rather than attach themselves to the Establish-
ment.

5. The immense revenues of the English and
Scottish Establishments alone constitute a great
argument against their continuance; because
those reyenues, though the common, property
of the whole nation, are distributed among the
religious teachers of half, or loss than half, of the
people. Enormous and disproportionate salaries

FEB. 10, 1872.

and emoluments are paid to _Bishops and other,
Dignitaries, while, of that portion of the fund
which is received by the parochial olergy, by fur
the largest part falls to those who have the fewest.
parishioners, and the smallest to such as minister
among the densest populations.
6. The obstructiveness of the Establishment is ,
an additional reason for abolishing it. Its bishops "
and clergy are neither appoiated nor controlled by,
nor are they responsible to, the People. JealottS:
of their own privileges, they resist all changes
which may affect their own ascendancy, or that ofy
the Establishment in which they have so strong a
vested interest. Hence, in every agitation of a,
political or social character, they are always 401,
one side and the People on the other. .1
7. The Establishment is a source of nationaL
weakness, because it divides the nation into two
hostile parties. It prevents good men uniting, ss
they otherwise might unite, in works of philail-
ithropy and in movements for social reform.
thus carries a mischievous rieetarianism into almost
all the affairs of life.

Such are the questions which the Committee of,
Working Men commend to the serious consideratioe.,
of their fellow workmen throughout the country.
In order to ascertain and give effect to their views,
Branch Committees will be formed, and MeetitlgS
held, in all the large towns. It is hoped, and believed,'
that the practical result will be that, after this,
great question has been submitted to the electors,
when it is next slebated in the House of Commons,
Mr. Miall will be in a position to give to Mr.
Gladstone's challenge a satisfactory and decisivo
answer.—We are, on behalf of the Working
Men's Committee, Yours faithfully,
Gxonaz Holm', (Chairman).
DANIEL Gutrx (Treasurer).
GEORGE POTTER (Secretary).
