and will introduce a simple and still more
effective measure than the last.
On the subject of the new Licence Bill,
Ministers are fairly warned, that if, in their
forthcoming measure, they east the brewers
and the publicans overboard, noble lords and
right honourable gentlemen on the opposite
side of the question will not see such important
interests submerged without taking credit for
an attempt at least to rescue them. " I trust,"
said his Grace of ItrerruoND, " Tier Majesty's
Government, in putting down intoxication, will
not lose sight of the fact that there are large
classes in the country whose interests must
not be neglected. Lord DERBY
.admitted the
difficulties of the question, and only ventured
to suggest to Mr. BRUCE, not to aim at
too much, and think, not only of .the interests
immediately concerned, but also of those
social habits and popular feelings which will
have to be taken into consideration, and con-
tent themselves rather with what the great
majority of persons consider glaring and ob-
vious abuses than aim at the passing of a com-
plete and comprehensive measure.
The alleged decrease of crime in Ireland

was subjected to criticism, The Earl ol
DERBY seemed to intimate an opinion thai

the appearance might be due to a system of
intimidation so complete and successful as to
require no more outrages for its full effect.
Lard PowEnscounr illustrated the reference
to Ireland with his own local knowledge.
That country, he said, had never before been so
prosperous as she was now. Her shorthorns
and other stock were admitted to be nearly as
good as any in England. The animal which
Obtained the gold cup at the show of the
Royal Agricultural Society last year was bred
and fed in the county of Cork. In fine, he
believed that English capital was only waiting
to see the result of the Home Rule movement

before seeking large employment in Ireland.

The introduction of an Education Bill for
Sootland is the only measure of that kind
Promised by Ministers. Mr. COLMAN', who
son4led the Address, was independent
onCngh to say, that religious teaching was
best left to the free will of Christian people.
in saying this, he fully sympathised with the
Position in which the Government was placed
When the measure was under discussion.
Nonconformists at that time were not at one.
Ro was not prepared to say that every Non-
conformist agreed with him at the present
time; but the principles they advocated were
gro'iving daily in the country. He ventured
to hope that when the question again came on
for discussion, they should be able to discuss
their differences fairly and temperately, with
_ .

view to such a solution as would bring eau-

cation home to every child in the realm.
The omission of education in Ireland from
the list of sessional measures was observed

upon is perhaps showing that nothing would
be attempted this year. Lord DERI3I7 warned
Ministers that putting off rarely facilitated
settlement.

Other omissions of the Speech were too eon-
spieuous by absence not to have been made
ground of party attaek. Not ono word is .
said about either army or navy. And yet
the Megrera was sent to sea with a bottom no
thicker than a newspaper, and of course wont
down, while, on evidence taken before the
Commission, at the Admiralty itself, every
thing has boon destroyed and nothing re-

towed, As for the army, instead of re-
organising it and educating it in a single
Parliamentary recess (all of which, of course,
would certainly have been done had the Duke
RICII3IOND and Mr. DisniEu been in
Power), nothing visible has been accomplished.
The obvious answer of Earl GRANVILLE was,

that, as to the Megfera and other naval
matters, the Government would consider what
should be done when the Commissioners had
made theirreport, which hasnocyot been agreed
upon. With respect to the Army, such steps have
been taken as were practicable; but any sub-
stantial improvements must of necessity wait
until the House of Conunons have 'voted the
needful means.
The FORETG N' SECRETARY stated pretty
plainly the view taken by Ministers with re •
ferenee to France. They make no pretence to
teach her rulers their duty whether their
policy should be in accordance with the views'
held amongst us now, or with those many
years ago entertained by eminent persons.
We feel, said the noble FlAnf., that with every
desire to meet every just requirement, it
would not be right to take part in any retro-
grade movement. • We believe we ought to
, leave France to take her own course. Mean-
time, every political relation with France has
been undisturbed, and any slight differences
of opinion have been satisfactorily adjusted.
On this subject it was opportunely stated by
Mr. Cor,EmArf that the total trade in imports
and exports between the United Kingdom and
France for 1859 was 261- millions, and for
1869 the returns were nearly 57 millions,
showing an increase of more than 30 millions
sterling, or 113 per cent.

As a matter of course, Ministers are to
blame for not so arranging the Washington
Treaty as to preclude the swelling of Ameri-
can claims ; as if any precaution, with or
without the co-operation of Sir STAFFORD
NORTHCOTE who sits with the Opposition,
could have prevented our cousins from adding
to their little bill any items they might think
of or imagine. On this point the DUKE of
RICHMOND inquired whether Ministers made
an immediate reply. "My Lords,'.' answered
Earl GRANVILLE, "[am happy to say we did
no such thing; for, unless for preventing im-
mediate evil, any differences between countries
ought to be dealt with calmly and with deli-
beration, so as not to throw away the smallest
chance of an amicable agreement, On the
whole, we thought it would do more to soothe
irritation here, and to prevent the possible
envenoming of discussion hereafter; would
strengthen our position, and be more straight-
forward and frank to the United States, for us
to send a communication of the general
character indicated in her MAJESTY'S Speech.
Last year I made a statommt with respect to
the interpretation Government put upon the
Treaty; I recited the direct claims in the first
protocol of Mr. Frsrr, and I made the remark,
that many of the claims under the Stanley
Convention had entirely disappeared, and had
been closed by the treaty. It is our opinion

now. That establishes beyond doubt what was
the intention of Government and of the Com-
missioners. This is not the time to go into
the argument; but I trust I shall be able
to show to the American Government, by refer-
°nee to different parts of the Treaty, by the
protdeols, by communications which passed,
by the statements of the Commissionms, and
by the previous correspondence, not only what
was our intention, but also what we had
reason to believe was the intention of the
United States. Lastly, I hope to be able to
show that these claims were excluded by the
Treaty itself. I trust, moreover, that the
American people, with that shrewd sense so
characteristic of them, will see the impossi-
bility of our referring to any tribunal, how-
ever high, claims so large and so indefinite."

Lord DERBY attributed the mischief to the
sending out of a special Commisson. When
that negotiation was entered into, we were in
a position absolutely unassailable. We had
repaired our original error and had offered a
reference on fair and equal terms which had
been rejected by the Senate and the House of
Representatives. But, having made that offer,
we had put ourselves in the right, and it was
our duty to remain in that position, only
telling the United States, that the offer they
had rejected was still open to their acceptance.
What more fair, more natural, more obvious,
than to say, " Very well, you rojeat our pro -
position, we will net make another; it is your
turn now, and, if you make one, we will con-
sider whether we can accept it or not P " We
diAl not do that but wo sent out a speoial COM-

mission to Washington, to demonstrate to the
world the extreme importance we attached to
the settlement of the question. The natural
result was it gave a Strong hint to the American
Government end people that they might safely
their terms, without any fear of the negotia-
tions being broken off, a hint • that they
were not likely to be slow in adopting.
We cannot be surprised that the •American
negotiators, who had found that the more they
asked the more they got, should play again
the same game. Whether we ever had a
chance of making a good bargain he did not
know; but he is quite sure, that if we ever
had it, we have lost it, as men very often lose
such chances, by kotooing and protruding
their anxiety to obtain a settlement of a dis-
pute. Lord DERIN does, however, agree with
the Government, that these new claims are
not, and never were, included in the Treaty.
It is quite enough for us to to know what was
our meaning, what we intended to offer, what
• we believed, we were offering. , To that, wise
or unwise, we are bound to adhere, but to
nothing more. On the other hand, if both
sides have been unintentionally misleading
one another, then the essential element of a
contract is wanting, and the negotiation is 4t
an end. That Lord DERBY understands to bo
the contention or the Government, and he
holds they are fully justified. In dealing
with the American negotiators, they will have
the undivided support of every party and of
every class. But the more firm and unyield-
ing we are in a dispute of Ulla sort, the more
we are bound to use those international
courtesies of language and expression which
smooth many difficulties, and never weaken
an argument.

The speech of Mr. Drsnaur was, as usual,
an over-acted part. After attacking the
Government with affected bitterness, he
tenderod to them a hypocritical support.
Perhaps, however, neither the LORD CIIAN-
CELLOR nor the PRINIE MINISTER feels himself
in need of the help. All was to the advantage of
ajsineere and earnest man like Mr. GLADSTONE,
who, without any harshness towards the United
States, repudiated the idea of entertaining
any claim for indefinite consequential damages,
in which he had the manifest support of the
whole House.

The Government notices are for the intro-
duction of the Mines Regulation Bill on the
12th instant, of a Scotch Education Bill on the
same day; of a Bill to rep3al the Contagious
Diseases Act, on the 13th; of the Ballot Bill,
on the 14th; of a Corrupt Practices Amend-
ment Bill, on the same day; of a Bill relating
to the public health, on the 16th.

The notices of motion given by independent
Members are,--Mr. GOURLEY on the Dock.

yards, March 10; Mr. MICFIE on the number
of British subjects becoming aliens in foreign
parts, Feb. 20; by Mr. R. N. FOWLER on the
Coolie Traffic, Feb. 16; Mr. DIXON "on the
Elementary Education Act, March 5; Mr.
GILPIN, to move the Abolition of Capital
Punishments, Feb. 0; Mr. P. Tamon, of a
Bill to Repeal the Game Laws, Feb. 14; Mr.
COWPER TEMPLE, of a Bill to enable persons
not in orders to preach in Churches, Feb. 20.

THE PROGRAMME OF THE SESSION.
THE QUEEN'S Speech is one of the most
wordy of a wordy class. The first three
paragraphs having been given to the subject
of the illness and recovery of the PRINCE, and
to the Thanksgiving on his account, a larger
number than usual are spent upon foreign
affairs. To the customary assurance that all
is right betwixt ourselves and other Powers,
succeeds first an enormous paragraph on the
slave trading in Polynesia, the killing of
Bishop: PATTESON, and the means to be used
for punishing or preventing such atrocities.
The more strictly foreign affairs brought in
are our relations with France and America.
As to the former Republic, a divergence of
views regarding "the value of Protective
laws," is stated to have hindered "any agree-
ment to modify" the Commercial Treaty, in
spite of an earnest desire on both sides to
keep up friendship between the two nations.
In a series of four paragraphs, the threatened
hitch in the execution of the Washington
Treaty is dealt with. .The English ease and
the American case have both been laid before

the arbitrators at Geneva. The former is now
described; the latter includes "large claims
understood," says the QUEEN, "on Illy part
not to be within the province of the arbi-
trators." Her 11.t.rEsry has, therefore, caused
a friendly communication to be made to the
Governmentof the United States.
• The domestic section of the Speech starts
with Ireland, as, with very few exceptions,
free from serious crime, and as enjoying an
active trade, with a remarkable advance in
rural industry. In Great Britain also, "pre-
sent experience" shows a "perceptible di-
minution" of grave crimes and of habitual
criminals. The estimates for the coming year
are to be at once laid before the Commons,
who, it is hoped, will find them suitable to
the circumstances of the country. The state
of the revenue, in the meantime, together
with a decline of pauperism not inconsiderable,
indicates more work for hands and more food
for mouths.

That section of the Speech which refers to
future legislation is the shortest, simplest, and
least pretending. The first of the "several
measures of acknowledged national interest"
announced is an Education Bill for Scotland;
the second, one for the Regulation of Mines;
the third, for the amendment of the Licensing
of Public-houses ; with a fourth relating to
the superior courts of justice and appeal, and
more than one for administrative improve-
ment in Ireland. Promise is made also of
"legislative provisions founded upon the report
of the Sanitary Commission." The only purely
political measures announced, are a Ballot
Bill and a Corrupt Practices at Parliamentary
Elections Bill; which two will ho immediately
presented. In fine, the two houses are ex-
horted to apply themselves with their " well -
known assiduity to that work of legislation
which, from the increasing exigencies of
modern society, still seems to grow upon ttieir
hands."

articles.text:
PROSELYTISL

A cunrotrs light is thrown on the education
controversy by a trial which took place a few
days since in the Court of Queen's Bench.
The facts are simple enough. hull. BARRETT,
a policeman, died, leaving five children.
Three were provided for and two were sent to
Wbitechapel Workhouse, and afterwards re-
moved from.thcnoe to St. Mary's Orphanage, a,

10

Roman Catholic establishment. The father
clearly wished to have his children brought
up in the Police Orphanage, should such
necessity arise, as he had subscribed for that
purpose when alive. When there was room
in this Orphanage, application was made for the
child, JAMES BAultErr, and in consequence Of I
this a suit in the Queen's Bench flowed; the
result being that the child had to be given up,by
the managers of the Catholic Orphanage. '
Now the wonder is, that a case like this
should ever arise. If there were only a 'few
score poor children without natural protectors
capable of providing for them, it would not be
difficult to understand - why zealous people
should quarrel about them with the view of
saving them from the sad fate of our poor infant,
waifs and strays. But when we know there,
are hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands',
who may be had for the asking, for the mere
trouble of picking up, we naturally feel
surprise when we read of litigants, lawyers,
and judges, fighting, arguing, and solemnly
giving judgment in such a case as this. Were
it not very sad, it would be rather funny to see
that in the same week, and whilst this trial
was going on, a deputation of the School
Board waited on Mr. Bar cal, with regard
to making, if possible, provision for a Multi-
tude of " gutter children," an, expensive
contention should be going on in the Celia ,
of Qneen's Bench for. the possession of one
child, regardless of this multitude of unpro-
vided-for little ones. ,
The ease being given againt the Roman
Catholic Orphanage, will very likely be looked
on as a persecution. But, if a" row" is not
what they aim at about this child, lost to
them on a point of law, they may apply to
the Sehool Board, and there can be little
doubt they may have ten or a dozen about the
possessien of whom nobody will trouble them.;
Unhappily, zealots in religion like to light.
Froiii the commencement of the world, in ,
every faith, on every quarter of the globe, I
they have always been ready when a colour-
able cause could be found; and when no cause
existed, their ingenuity in creating one has
been, and still is, very remarkable. Protestant
an Catholic run at each other through a kind
of pugnacious instinct, which neither have the
good sense to control.

What are you fighting about, you two?
Why! my eyes are grey, and his are blue.
Pooh ! pooh! youbloolcheads--stand away.
Not till he changes his eyes to blue !
Not till he changes his eyes to grey!
It appears from the statement of Mr. Dinar Arr,
that there is a, priest named Father SEDDEN,
whosebusiness it is to go abouthunting up these
children in all t 4 workhouses in London, and
a profitable job this is,, no doubt, for
the lawyers, but if Mr. Bunn= andhis friends
will advertise in the rime* or Zlegrayh, we
arc sure they will get a larger, number of
children by spending a pound, than if they
spent a hundred in, ths Court of cancan's
Bench, and will at the same time, avoid the
scandal attaching to such utterly anti-Chris-
tian antics.

We. must, not forget, however, that the
intensified feeling of bigotry thus manifested,
is what places the chief stambling.block in the
way of a good system, of national edueation.
It burns like fire in the bosom of the Catholic
Church, Land is just as active, though not with
so much constancy and method, amongst our
zealous Protestants, who are indignant at the
obstinacy of their Papistical

"That the Pope is still a datholie most plainly
doth aPPeari
And we therefore hate him famously, apa fearfully
do fear,
For they say his troops are creel Bulls, and that
they're coming over,
AM they'll run about and toss us all, unless we
stop up Dover;
Ncrw we'd lot him turn a Protestant—so it's quite
a shame ho don't,
Ana it shows what a base man he is, when he
might be one and won't.
A. moderately good system of national educa-
tion would gradually put an end to such
stupid folly as this. But with a Government
afraid to offend any party by attempting to
frame such a measure, we must be content to
go on until our moral, politiCal, and industrial
requirements force Us into com Mon-sense pro-
ceedings, and into , a belief that Christian
charity, and a sincere respect for religious truth
are not necessarily antagonistic.

articles.title: AMERICAN "CASE."
articles.text:
THE AMERICAN "CASE."

TILE tone of communications from the
Amerioe.n shore is, on the whole, not unfavour-
able to the hope of a favourable settlement of
claims between England and the United
Stats. The actual form of the American
case cannot be mistaken, but we are told, on
perhaps adequate authority, that, in the
official circle at Washington, payment fo-
indirect or consequential damages is•not seri-
ously expected. One of the New York journals
remarks sensibly enough,, that the question
will be settled by the arbitrators and not by
either the Governments or the Press of the
two countries. Some of those journals that
charge our contemporaries with stirring up
excitement, commit the same error on their
side; though the Herald, as Usual, enjoys the
distinction of recklessly provoking to the last
extremity.

It is pretty clear that the messageafrom our
Government, followed by the moderation of
the: QUEEN'S Speech, caused a subsidence of
excitement in Washington and at Now York.
It was understood that in our view the clues:.
tion of indirect damages was not to be arbi-
trated. upon, and it was observed that the note
said nothing about receding from the Treaty.
This is the tone of those persons and papers
that will really influence opinion on the other
side.

Mr. GLA.DSTONE has shown -the largeness of
our coneessiOns, and has endeavoured to
justify them; as showing a determination that,
national honour and rut tional safety made sure,
nothing should stand in the Way of that
cordial amity which it is desirable to set as an
example before the world. But there
must be somewhere or other a cloie to all
such procedure. There is evidence on one side,
quoted. by• Americans themselves, that
Ministers of the British Crown .explicitly
declared the exclusion by the Anieriattn Go-
vernment of claims for indirect losses, and, as
the PREMIER tells us, there has come
no protest from Washington against those de-
clarations. The QuEnw's Ministers, therefore,
take their stand upon no ambiguity of expres-
sion, real or supposed, but upon the plain ground
that the indirect claims are understood by
them not to. be subjects of arbitration. "A
man," said Mr. GLADSTONE on Tuesday night,
" must be insane, a nation must be insane to
suppose that we .'should admit impossible
claims of this character in a peaceful arbitra-
tion, which, not even in the last eirtremity of
war, not even in the lowcst depths of mitt.
fortune, a people with a spark of spirit, with
a hundredth part of theitraditions and courage
of the people of this country, would consent,
at the point of death, to admit, I look
forward with .n sanguine hope as to the course
which the American Government May take on
thie 'matter.", If we think they aro pressing
us hardly on an occasion like this, yet they
have given us signs and tokens of friendship
which cannot be mistaken. On Wednesday,
under
,new instigation, Mr. GLA.DSTONE ex-
ceeded himself in impressiveness and decision
of tone. ; This second speech, at any rate,
is conclusive. For what, asit shows them, are
the facts of the matter 1' The Protocol of the
9th of March declares, on behalf of the Arne-
rican Commissioners, ,f that, in the hope of
an amicable settlement, no estimate was made
of the indirect Josses, Without prejudice,. !WV'
aver, to the right indemnification on their ac-
count in the event of no such settlernentibeing
made." In justification of the re-introduetion
of these abandoned claims, it has been alleged.
.that the Arbitration is not an amicable settle-
ment. But this is conclusively refuted by the
preamble to the Treaty, " Her Britannic
MAJESTY and the 'United States of America,
,being desirous to provide for an amicable set-
tlement of all causes of difference between the
two countries, have for that purpose appointed
their respective Plenipotentiaries," &e„. In
the American "Case" however, the Treaty is
quoted with the omission 0C this' preamble. If
the compilers had remembered it, claims for
indirect d ainageti must have disappeared, The
Protocol and preamble make it clear that. the
Treaty and the Arbitration are :that amicable
settlement in consideration of "which indirect
losses were waived. The preamble ia omitted
from the British Case also, because the revival
of pretensions unequivocally renounce (1 could.

not have presented itself to our Government
and its agents. When the American Govern-
ment and people have the terms of the pre-
amble recalled to their recollection, they will
promptly accede to the British interpretation,
and withdraw the claim which inadvertence
only could have led them to prefer.

articles.text:
TRADES 'UNIONS.

TILE Northern Whig in an article in its
issue on the 17th ultimo, on the paper
read by Mr. GUILE at Nottingham, on Trades
Unions, after a good deal of banter, says:—
" We, have
.never been amongst those
who have unreasonably decried Trades
Unions. , While they have doubtless done
much harm to both employers and employed,
they are capable, if rightly organised and
managed, of doing not n little good. But the
spirit which presides over them must be a
spirit very different, to that indicated by Mr.
GUILE in the paper to which we have. referred.
It is time that we had heard* the
.last of the
"avaricious, grasping capitalist " whom Mr.
GUILE seems constantly to have in his mind
as the natural enemy of , the oppressed work-
ing man, There may have been, and there
may be still, fiitoti avaricious, grasping capital-
ists; but those. who .so, freely use
.these
epithets should learn to weigh their:words, a
little more carefully, and especially' to bethink
themselves whether it is quite just to make
such a sweeping cendemutition of all capitalists
aB "avaricious and grasping." ,
To this article Mr. Guile sent the following
sensible reply :

articles.title: TO TIIE EDITOR OF TEE NORTRERN wlizo.
articles.text:
TO TIIE EDITOR OF TEE NORTRERN wlizo.

" hope, as you have taken the trouble
in Your very popular paper to treat me to a very
severe castigation, that you will allow me a little
space in reply. In your issue for Wednesday,
Jenuary 17th, You say a certain Mr. Guile read a
paper which hardly seems to be guileless. This
conceive to be an error of yours; for, if you will
take the trouble to read the paper, you will find
that there is no guile in it ;that it is not in the least
clothed in anything like the garb of Whig diplo-
macy, but is outspoken and plain, and hence, in
your opinion, deserves the, treatment you have
been pleased to belabour it with. Now, it is a
maxim not only. in England but all, aver the
world, "that 'au Englishman is a lover of fair
play. This scarcely appears the case with the
editor of the Northern Whig, But I suppose,
fair-play to a working man is a thing
of no consideration with those who are
paid to, uphold the interest of the avari-
cious grasping capitalist, and, as you seem to
have that disease on the brain, I must suppose
that you could see nothing else in the paper ex-
cepting the mania you appear to be afflicted with.
In your paper you make it appear that I set down
all employers in the'same category. This I deny
most dmphtitically. I thank God that there are in
this country employers who, for kindness to their
employes, liberldity in remunerating them for
w ork, and many other 'virtues, cannot be excelled
in the world ; but, while you castigate me for
alluding to avaricious grasping capitalists, you
admit, almost in the same breath, that there
' may be such employers. We working men know
there are such, and as such we shall try to treat
them. I have no apology to offer for the expres-
sions I used in my paper, and all I ask of you is
that you exeroise that fair 'play which I think
every man deserves—viz., that you give the
whole paper, as read by,ine at the Trades' Congresa
—and then I shall be prepared to submit to any
censure either employer, workman, or yourself May
think tit to pass upon me. If you refuse to do this,
then I can only say that your critique is as unfair
as it would be to take two passages out of Sacred
Writ, and judge the Holy Book by those passages;
which are—‘ He went out and hung himself;'
go thou and d 9 likewise.' We are always
glad to receive advice from such men as Mr.
Auberon Herbert, who, it seems, has pleased you

THE DILIE DE NIONSTRA.TION IN

TRAFALGAR SQUARE.

An open air meeeting took place on Monday
evening in Trafalgar-square, for the purpose
of expressing sympathy with Sir Charles Mike,
upholding freedom of speech, and generally
asserting the right of public meeting. Lime
lights were displayed from the balustrades in
front of the National Gallery, and the whole'
of the space ,
between them and the Nelson
Column W s with a dense mass of people.
The various processions began to arrive atsoelveesn,
o'clock. They, were accompanied by banners
with caps of liberty at the tops of the p
and bearing a variety of Republican inscriptions.

Republican flag had been set up, and at the
corners were, standard-bearers with red flags.
Mr. Oclger arrived at the time appointed, and
was greeted with loud cheering. The business
at once commenced, amid the surging noise
that is generally noticed at open air meetings.
The Chairman began by stating that it was
not the wish of those with whom he acted to have
• held that demonstration, bat their opponents ,
had forced it upon them. England, as his
hearers were aware, had long been boasted of
as , being a country governed under a
thoroughly representative system. Now, there
were considerable numbers of the people of
the country who had long been desirous of
making the representative system as pure and as
real as possible, and in order to do this asso-
ciations had sprung up in different parts of the
country, haying for their object direct and un-
mistakeably representative Government. These
associations had held Meetings, and they had
the right to invite' persons to come and address
them (chee' rs) • and the Democrats had as
much right to cici this as the Conservatives, or
the Whigs, or the Radicals. He held it would
be a piece of very bad conduct on the part of
the Democrats if they were to prevent the
Conservatives from hearing Lord Derby, Mr.
Disraeli, or Lord Stanley; but then the'
,others did not have the same sense of justice
which animated the Democrats. The Demo-
crats had a right to invite one of the most
peaceful, one of the most earnest, one of the
most honourable men in the House of Com-
mons to their' meeting, and he, beeause he
analyzed the civil list, was held to have insulted
the Queen, and a great sensation had been
created because he had shown how the money,
of the nation was squandered. Scarcely had
that speech at Newcastle been made,. before the
Whig proprietor of a newspaper, Mr. Edward
Baines, of Leeds, became the first hound in the
hunt against a man as far his superior as it
was possible for one man to be above another.
But Sir Charles Dilke was not to be thus put
down, and he went to Leeds. There some five
hundred Tories would have broken up the
meeting, but some five thousand Demeerats
told them not to attempt it, and this was a
specimen how the right of freedom of speech
was infringed.
Mr. Wynne moved the first resolution, as
follows :--
f 4 That this meeting, believing that the un-
trammelled exercise of the right of free speech
to discuss any political or social subject is an
absolute. essential to the condition of liberty in, ,
any country, hereby expressos its fixed deter-
mination to use every legitimate means in its
power to prevent the recurrence of those scents
which to the disgrace of this -country have bean
enacted at Bolton, Reading, Derby, and else.
where."

The speaker contended that the right of
public, meeting was inalienable from English-
men and Englishmen were determined to
maintain it.

Mr. Lelabez Esoeonded the resolution, wkioli't
was es.rriod.

Mr. Shipton moved, and Mr. Longmead so.
conded the, second resolution, which was also
carried:--

"That this meeting is of opinion that the eon.
duct of certain magistrates of-Bolton'doserves-the
gravest censure in not affording due protection to

and earnestly requested to send a force necessary
to gap it. And this meeting calls upon the
Item° Secretary te rot:love such magistrates from

The third 'resolution was moved by Mr•

carried:—

,
"That this meeting is of opinion that no real
step in the path of.politieal progress can be taken
until all 'Hereditary privileos ' in the State

est thanks of this meeting are due, and are

clergy, not only publicly to profess belief in

believe it sincerely in their hearts. M.

remain a priest and a Catholic, but a Catholic

Several other members of Parliament have met
their constituents since the list of last week, but
their 'utterances on the Criminal Law Amendment
AA have either been nil, or of so uncertain a cha-
racter that little can be made out of them. They
have not yet began to realise the fact that we are
in earnest.

Colonel Boresford, 3.1. P., met his constituents at

the Trades Union Act was, on the whole, beneficial.
Oa the 31st ult., 111 r. Leeman mot his constitu-

the subject at all.

Mr. IL .B. Samuelson at a meeting held at

The three members for Glasgow, Mr. Dalglisb,
Mr. Graham, and Mr. Anderson, met their con-
stituents on the Ist inst., but there seems to

Amendment Act and the Lords Amendment.
Surely Glasgow will not permit this question to
be ignored? Let our Glasgow friends see to it.
Sir Edward Bailer's only reference to trades
unions was that of defending the Government for
taking a non-union man, in the person of Sir
Robert Collier, into its pay for special service, the

the Trades Union Act and the Criminal Act of
last session.

Mr. Itoger Eykyn addressed his constituents al

with reference to our questions.
Sir J. C. Lawrence, Mr. Win. McArthur,
members for Limbetb, and the lion. Locke King,
for East Surrey, met their constituents on the sth
inst., but the allusions to these lets wore chiefly
incidental, except Sir J. Lawrence, who stated
that he strenuously opposed the Lords' Amend-
ments.

The chief utterances will now be Parliamentary,
all of which we shall note. The Minos Regula-
tion Bill is promised early, but no reference in
the Queen's Speech is made to the Truok Bill.
We shall got the Arbitration Bill in hand at an
early date, and consult as to the best man to pro-
pose the repeal of tho Criminal Law A.mendment
Act.

Gronon llowaLL,
Secretary of the Parliamentary Committee.

CHURCH REFORM MEETING IN
ST. JAMES'S HALL.
To [the Editor of the BEE-Hrer.
Sm,--It is reported that a meeting is to ne
held in St. James's llall, on the 15th inst.,
8 pan., at which four resolutions are to be
moved, of the following naturet—(l) That 5
reformation bathe Church le necessary to save
it from disestablishment. (9) That the laity
should have some voice in the introduction
of changes within the law. (8) That
smaller quantity of the Prayer Book Services
should be administered at one sitting.
(4) That the Athanasian Creed should not be
used any longer. So that, the putting awe,'
of one creed or doctrine, as a damnatory
spirit, seems to be the chief reformation
aimed at by this meeting because the
Church already has liberty to shorten the
services, as there is not any Act of Parliareenu

commonly are, at one sitting.
, Well, if this creed or doctrine were the on
damnatory one in the Church to be cast out!
the putting it away would indeed be a grea
reformation. But if. the Church continues te
retain (as it does) other doctrines equally as
evil and even worse, then there is not anY
reformation accomplished by the mere casting
out of this creed as may be seen in 2.
moment; e.g., if pAlicans agreed to leave o
selling rum or whishy on a Sunday,e
would
this satisfy any member of a temperance
society, whilst the publicans continued to giv°
out or sell other spirits of as great or greater
strength, and in greater quantity P Ant
would it be any satisfaction to the members 01
a temperance Bode!). that the publicans allowed
them "some voice in. the introduction of ohanitts
in the spirits . within the card or list they-
served ? " Why, the mere changing or one

ciety whilst the publicans doggedly refused to

societies. And neither is it any reformation

receive others which are worse; in
her doctrine of atonement she images God, the
Holy Spirit, to have been a spirit of evil,
a doer of evil, and an approver of evil; and
she corrupts the Scriptures, which are good, to
support such evil doctrines, audthen doggedly
and tyrannically refuses to open the national
houses (dedicated to God's service) for the ser-
vice of any other than these evil doctrines.
But as temperance societies organize to save
the people from intoxicating spirits, the peopl.e
should organize and determine to save their
children's souls from evil and false doctrines
by compelling "the State" to open the pulp t 3
of the National Church, wit hout.favour or fear,
to such ordained ministers as have aught to
tell the people of Jesus, as the Church at
Antioch was opened for the people to hear St.
Paul.

This opening of the pulpit is the reforma-
tion requtred, and then what is truth of the
Church's doctrines will be submitted to the
piercing gaze of the people, and the jler9
ordeal of public opinion ; and what is not truth
will then be as patent to the people as th°
merits of the respective witnesses in the Tich-
borne trial. And as no one but impostors

lot the clergy (without requiring. compulsion)
voluntarily open their pulpits Id the abov!

T. G. HEADLEY.
